steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on CAGE, a framework that automatically learns category trees for ID-only recommendation datasets using differentiable vector quantization.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Recommender systems and their objectives
- Value of categorical information
- Missing categories in ID-based recommendation; CAGE
- Limits of previous VQ methods; differentiable VQ
- Granularity; cascaded VQ
- Summary of advantages

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Recommender systems
  - ease decision-making, personalized recommendations from preferences and history
  - objectives: list completion, collaborative filtering, click-through rate prediction
  - need methods adaptable to different scenarios
- Categorical information
  - very important in model design
  - product types, user locations: capture attributes, connect users and items
  - mitigate cold-start: extra info for less active (sparsely interacting) users/items
  - refined by active entities' interactions during training -> more robust representations
- CAGE
  - many datasets only have IDs, no categories
  - automatic category tree generation framework (CAGE); assumption: hierarchical categories common at varying scales
  - Figure 1: precursor to recommender, builds item/user category tree, hierarchical knowledge ("Good", "Gaming") for entity ("I-123")
  - category vectors given to recommender as auxiliary info with user/item ID
  - based on differentiable and cascaded vector quantization (VQ)
- Previous VQ methods
  - rely on meaningful, fixed entity embeddings from side info (content-aware item embeddings, pretrained models)
  - three-stage design (Figure 2): representation learning, VQ, recommendation training separately
  - no side info in ID-based -> no meaningful embeddings early -> impractical
  - differentiable VQ: entity embeddings and codebook vectors adjusted via recommendation tasks + quantization constraints, from random init to robust, stable form
- Granularity
  - fine categories -> data sparsity; coarse -> hide differences between entities
  - cascaded VQ -> category tree with varying granularity
  - vs single-layer category systems in datasets: hierarchical taxonomy, more comprehensive
- Advantages
  - i. end-to-end: unlike multi-stage VQ, first to explore differentiable VQ end-to-end for category generation without side info; categorization aligned with objectives for items and users
  - ii. easy adoption: pluggable into sequential and non-sequential models; list completion, collaborative filtering, CTR prediction
  - iii. effectiveness: evaluation on multiple tasks, tem datasets, 14 baselines; significant improvements in most scenarios; up to 21.41% relative improvement in list completion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recommender systems try to make decision-making easier by automatically suggesting personalized item recommendations that fit a user's preferences and historical behavior. They have diverse objectives like list completion, collaborative filtering, and click-through rate prediction. Because the objectives are so varied, it is important to design methods that can adapt to different recommendation scenarios and give better recommendations.

When designing recommendation models and algorithms, it is very important to integrate categorical information. Categorical attributes like product types and user locations are widely used, because they capture crucial attributes and make meaningful connections for users and items. These category features also help with the cold-start problem, since they give an additional layer of information for less active (sparsely interacting) entities (i.e., users or items). This extra information gets refined during training by interactions from active users or items, which helps less active entities get more robust representations.

But category features are not always available, because many recommendation datasets only have ID information. To deal with missing category attributes in ID-based recommendation, we propose a new automatic category tree generation framework called CAGE. We assume that hierarchical categorical structures commonly come up in recommendation scenarios of different scales. Figure 1 shows that CAGE works as the precursor to the recommender system and dynamically builds an item/user category tree, which contains hierarchical categorical knowledge (e.g., "Good" and "Gaming") relevant to the current entity (e.g., "I-123"). The categorical information is encoded as vectors and given to the recommender system as auxiliary information together with the user/item ID. CAGE is implemented with differentiable and cascaded vector quantization (VQ).

- previous VQ methods: fixed entity embeddings from side info (pretrained models); three-stage design (Figure 2); impractical without side info
- differentiable VQ: embeddings and codebook vectors adjusted through recommendation tasks and quantization constraints, from random to robust, stable
- granularity: fine -> sparsity, coarse -> hides differences; cascaded VQ -> category tree with varying granularity; hierarchical vs single-layer
- advantages: i. end-to-end (first differentiable VQ without side info); ii. pluggable, sequential and non-sequential; iii. effectiveness - tem datasets, 14 baselines, up to 21.41% in list completion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recommender systems try to make decision-making easier by automatically suggesting personalized item recommendations that fit a user's preferences and historical behavior. They have diverse objectives like list completion, collaborative filtering, and click-through rate prediction. Because the objectives are so varied, it is important to design methods that can adapt to different recommendation scenarios and give better recommendations.

When designing recommendation models and algorithms, it is very important to integrate categorical information. Categorical attributes like product types and user locations are widely used, because they capture crucial attributes and make meaningful connections for users and items. These category features also help with the cold-start problem, since they give an additional layer of information for less active (sparsely interacting) entities (i.e., users or items). This extra information gets refined during training by interactions from active users or items, which helps less active entities get more robust representations.

But category features are not always available, because many recommendation datasets only have ID information. To deal with missing category attributes in ID-based recommendation, we propose a new automatic category tree generation framework called CAGE. We assume that hierarchical categorical structures commonly come up in recommendation scenarios of different scales. Figure 1 shows that CAGE works as the precursor to the recommender system and dynamically builds an item/user category tree, which contains hierarchical categorical knowledge (e.g., "Good" and "Gaming") relevant to the current entity (e.g., "I-123"). The categorical information is encoded as vectors and given to the recommender system as auxiliary information together with the user/item ID. CAGE is implemented with differentiable and cascaded vector quantization (VQ).

Previous vector quantization methods for recommendation often depend on meaningful and fixed entity (e.g., user or item) embeddings that come from side information, like content-aware item embeddings from pretrained models. They usually use a three-stage design, shown in Figure 2, where representation learning, vector quantization, and recommendation training are done separately. But in ID-based recommendation there is no side information, so meaningful entity embeddings cannot be generated in the initial training phase, and this approach is impractical. We solve this by using differentiable VQ. With it, both the entity embeddings and the categorical code vectors from the quantization codebooks are adjusted dynamically through recommendation tasks and quantization constraints. They start from random initial states and end up in a robust and stable form.

It is also crucial to choose the right level of detail for categories. Very detailed categories could cause data sparsity issues in the recommendation system, and broader, coarse-grained categories may hide important differences between entities. Because of this, we propose cascaded VQ to build a category tree with different levels of granularity. Datasets usually have a single-layer category system, but our cascaded approach creates a hierarchical taxonomy of categories, which represents entities more comprehensively.

To summarize, we introduce CAGE, an automatic category tree generation framework for ID-based recommendation, and it has several advantages and capabilities:

i. End-to-end framework. Unlike the usual multi-stage use of VQ in recommender systems, we are the first to explore differentiable VQ as an end-to-end solution for category generation without side information, i.e., ID-based recommendation. End-to-end training means the categorization for both items and users can be refined and optimized to match specific recommendation objectives.

ii. Easy adoption and high adaptability. CAGE is a pluggable module that can be easily integrated into both sequential and non-sequential recommendation models for different recommendation scenarios, including list completion, collaborative filtering, and click-through rate prediction.

iii. Effectiveness. We evaluate CAGE comprehensively on multiple recommendation tasks, including list completion, collaborative filtering, and click-through rate prediction. The evaluation uses tem datasets and compares with 14 baseline methods. The results show that CAGE is effective, with significant improvements in most scenarios. For example, CAGE has a relative improvement of up to 21.41% over state-of-the-art baselines in list completion tasks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recommender systems [1,2,3] aim to ease the burden of decision-making by automatically suggesting personalized item recommendations tailored to a user's preferences and historical behavior. They serve diverse objectives such as list completion, collaborative filtering, and click-through rate prediction. These varied objectives underscore the importance of methodologies that can adapt to different recommendation scenarios and deliver improved recommendations.

When designing recommendation models and algorithms, the integration of categorical information is of paramount importance. Categorical attributes, such as product types [4] and user locations [5,6], are widely used due to their ability to capture crucial attributes and establish meaningful connections for users and items. Furthermore, these category features help mitigate the cold-start problem, providing an additional layer of information for less active (sparsely interacting) entities (i.e., users or items) [7,8]. This supplementary information is progressively refined by interactions from active users or items during training, helping less active entities obtain more robust representations.

However, category features are not always available, since many recommendation datasets only have ID information. To address the absence of category attributes in ID-based recommendation contexts, we propose a novel automatic category tree generation framework, namely CAGE, under the assumption that hierarchical categorical structures commonly arise in recommendation scenarios of varying scales. As illustrated in Figure 1, CAGE serves as the precursor to the recommender system, dynamically constructing an item/user category tree that incorporates hierarchical categorical knowledge (e.g., "Good" and "Gaming") relevant to the current entity (e.g., "I-123"). The categorical information, encoded as vectors, is provided to the recommender system as auxiliary information alongside the user/item ID. CAGE is implemented with differentiable and cascaded vector quantization (VQ).

Previous vector quantization methods for recommendation [9,10] often rely on meaningful and fixed entity (e.g., user or item) embeddings, derived from side information such as content-aware item embeddings from pretrained models. They commonly adopt a three-stage design, as displayed in Figure 2, where representation learning, vector quantization, and recommendation training are carried out separately. However, the lack of side information in ID-based recommendation prevents the generation of meaningful entity embeddings during the initial training phase, making this approach impractical. We tackle this challenge by employing differentiable VQ [11], which enables dynamic adjustment of both entity embeddings and categorical code vectors from the quantization codebooks through recommendation tasks and quantization constraints, starting from their initial random states and resulting in a robust and stable form.

Moreover, it is crucial to select the appropriate level of detail for categories. Finely detailed categories could result in data sparsity issues within the recommendation system, while broader, coarse-grained categories may obscure significant differences among entities. To address this, we propose cascaded VQ to construct a category tree with varying levels of granularity. Unlike the single-layer category system commonly used in datasets, our cascaded approach creates a hierarchical taxonomy of categories, offering a more comprehensive representation of entities.

To summarize, we introduce CAGE, an automatic category tree generation framework for ID-based recommendation, which offers several notable advantages and capabilities:

i. End-to-end framework. Unlike the common multi-stage application of VQ in recommender systems [9,10], we are the first to explore differentiable VQ as an end-to-end solution for category generation in a scenario without side information, i.e., ID-based recommendation. Such end-to-end training allows the categorization of both items and users to be refined and optimized to align with specific recommendation objectives.

ii. Easy adoption and high adaptability. CAGE is a pluggable module that can be conveniently integrated into both sequential and non-sequential recommendation models to accommodate different recommendation scenarios, including list completion, collaborative filtering, and click-through rate prediction.

iii. Effectiveness. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of CAGE on multiple recommendation tasks, including list completion, collaborative filtering, and click-through rate prediction, involving tem datasets and a comparison with 14 baseline methods. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of CAGE, with significant improvements across most scenarios. For example, CAGE achieves a relative improvement of up to 21.41% over state-of-the-art baselines in list completion tasks.
